raw_text:
Sacubitril/valsartan is the prototypic angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), combining valsartan-mediated blockade of the angiotensin II type 1 receptor with sacubitril, a prodrug converted to the neprilysin inhibitor LBQ657 [1]. This dual action is biologically attractive in heart failure (HF): renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system inhibition attenuates vasoconstriction, sodium retention, hypertrophy and fibrosis, while neprilysin inhibition augments natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, adrenomedullin and related vasoactive peptides, promoting natriuresis, vasodilation and anti-remodelling effects [1,2]. Because neprilysin inhibition may increase angiotensin II, it must be paired with effective angiotensin receptor blockade rather than used alone [2].

The pivotal evidence in chronic HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) is PARADIGM-HF, which randomized symptomatic ambulatory patients with left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) ≤40% (later ≤35%) to sacubitril/valsartan or enalapril after sequential run-in [3]. Sacubitril/valsartan reduced the primary composite of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization, as well as cardiovascular and all-cause mortality [3]. Subsequent analyses showed less clinical progression among survivors, fewer sudden and pump-failure deaths, consistent efficacy across age groups, and preserved relative benefit even when doses were reduced below target [4-7]. These observations support ARNI as disease-modifying therapy rather than merely symptomatic treatment.

Safety and monitoring considerations are central to implementation. Compared with enalapril, sacubitril/valsartan causes more symptomatic hypotension but less cough, less hyperkalaemia and less renal impairment in several analyses [3,8,9]. In patients receiving mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, sacubitril/valsartan was associated with a lower risk of severe hyperkalaemia than enalapril [8]. BNP interpretation requires caution because BNP is a neprilysin substrate; NT-proBNP is generally preferred for monitoring, although BNP retains prognostic value after initiation [10]. Patient-centred benefits include modest but significant improvements in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire scores [11]. Additional post hoc data suggest improved glycaemic control in patients with diabetes, reduced loop diuretic requirements, fewer recurrent HF events, slower renal decline and fewer investigator-reported ventricular arrhythmias [12-16].

Several studies have informed initiation strategies. TITRATION demonstrated that both condensed and conservative up-titration regimens can be used, with slower titration helping patients previously receiving low-dose or no angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor/angiotensin receptor blocker therapy reach target doses [17]. In acute decompensated HFrEF, PIONEER-HF established that in-hospital initiation after haemodynamic stabilization produced greater NT-proBNP reduction than enalapril without excess renal dysfunction, hyperkalaemia or angioedema [18]. Benefit was seen across achieved dose levels [19]. TRANSITION further supported initiation either before discharge or soon after discharge, emphasizing hospitalization as an opportunity to optimize guideline-directed therapy [20].

Mechanistic and imaging studies complement clinical outcomes. PROVE-HF associated reductions in NT-proBNP after sacubitril/valsartan initiation with reverse cardiac remodelling, including improvements in LVEF and ventricular volumes [21]. EVALUATE-HF did not show a significant treatment effect on aortic impedance compared with enalapril, but it provided randomized data on vascular and cardiac structural measures during ARNI therapy [22]. Together, these studies suggest that biomarker improvement may reflect favourable myocardial remodelling rather than simple haemodynamic unloading.

The role of ARNI in HF with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction is more nuanced. PARAMOUNT showed greater NT-proBNP reduction with sacubitril/valsartan than valsartan in HFpEF, generating the rationale for outcome trials [23]. PARAGON-HF narrowly missed statistical significance for its primary endpoint in patients with LVEF ≥45%, but suggested greater benefit at lower LVEF and in women [24]. A pooled analysis across PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF supported a treatment gradient across LVEF, with benefit most apparent below the normal EF range [25]. PARAGLIDE-HF extended evaluation to recently worsened HF with LVEF >40%, showing greater NT-proBNP reduction versus valsartan [26]. Participant-level pooling of PARAGLIDE-HF and PARAGON-HF suggested reductions in cardiovascular and renal events, particularly among patients with LVEF below normal [27]. In PARAGON-HF, sacubitril/valsartan was also associated with reduced loop diuretic requirement, consistent with natriuretic effects [28].

Current US and European guidelines recommend sacubitril/valsartan as foundational therapy for symptomatic HFrEF, generally replacing an ACE inhibitor or ARB when tolerated; a 36-hour washout is required after ACE inhibitor use to reduce angioedema risk [29,30]. Practical barriers include hypotension, renal function, potassium abnormalities, cost, therapeutic inertia and underuse in older or comorbid patients. In contemporary care, ARNI should be integrated with beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors, using early initiation and iterative titration. Remaining questions include optimal sequencing, use in advanced kidney disease, interaction with emerging HFpEF therapies, and strategies to improve equitable uptake. Overall, sacubitril/valsartan represents a major advance in neurohormonal modulation, with definitive benefit in HFrEF and selective benefit across the mildly reduced/preserved EF spectrum.
